notes.front: What is security overview?
notes.back: A GitHub view giving insights into the security of code across an organisation’s or enterprise’s repositories, to identify those needing intervention.
notes.explanation: You find it on the Security and quality tab of an organisation or an enterprise.
notes.example: Like a head teacher’s dashboard of every class’s results, used to spot the classes that need extra help.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”
notes.evidence: You can gain insights into the overall security landscape of your organization or enterprise and identify repositories that require intervention using security overview. Security overview provides insights into the security of code stored in repositories in your organization.

notes.front: What is a security campaign?
notes.back: A way to group security alerts and share them with developers, so you can work together to fix vulnerabilities and exposed secrets.
notes.explanation: It is the step after identifying alerts: picking the most urgent ones and getting them fixed.
notes.example: Like a council’s pothole fortnight: the worst potholes are listed, crews are told, and progress is tracked to a deadline.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”
notes.evidence: Once you have identified security alerts the next step is to identify the most urgent alerts and get them fixed. Security campaigns are a way to group alerts and share them with developers, so you can collaborate to remediate vulnerabilities in the code and any exposed secrets.

notes.front: What is a campaign manager?
notes.back: A user or team chosen as a primary contact for a security campaign; it must be an organisation owner or a security manager.
notes.explanation: You can add an optional contact link, such as a GitHub Discussions page, for reaching the campaign managers.
notes.example: Like the named site supervisor on a building project, the person workers go to with questions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: Define a "Campaign due date" and select one or more "Campaign managers" as the primary contacts for the campaign. Campaign managers must be users or teams that are owners or security managers in the organization.

notes.front: What is a security alert timeline?
notes.back: An alert’s historical record of when it was created or the problem detected, and of every later status change.
notes.explanation: Status changes are recorded whatever caused them, and the timeline sits on the alert page under the problem’s description.
notes.example: Like a parcel’s tracking history: every scan and hand-over is logged, whoever did it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Security alert timelines”
notes.evidence: Each security alert has a historical timeline that shows when the alert was created or when a problem was detected. When the status of an alert changes this is recorded on the timeline, regardless of what caused the change

notes.front: What is a dismissal comment?
notes.back: An optional comment added when you dismiss an alert, kept on the alert timeline as justification for auditing and reporting.
notes.explanation: For a Dependabot alert, the comment is also available through the GraphQL API, in the `dismissComment` field.
notes.example: Like a note in a patient’s file explaining why a routine test was skipped, for anyone who reviews the case later.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing and updating Dependabot alerts”, “Dismissing Dependabot alerts”
notes.evidence: Optionally, add a dismissal comment. The dismissal comment will be added to the alert timeline and can be used as justification during auditing and reporting. You can retrieve or set a comment by using the GraphQL API. The comment is contained in the `dismissComment` field.

notes.front: Which branches do security overview’s views show information for?
notes.back: Only the default branches of the repositories you have permission to view.
notes.explanation: Alerts that exist only on other branches are not part of its figures.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: All views show information and metrics for the **default** branches of the repositories you have permission to view in an organization or enterprise.

notes.front: Security overview shows no alerts for a repository. What two explanations does GitHub give?
notes.back: Undetected vulnerabilities or code errors may still exist, or the feature may not be enabled for that repository.
notes.explanation: Security overview displays only the active alerts that security features have raised.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: Security overview displays active alerts raised by security features. If there are no alerts shown in security overview for a repository, undetected security vulnerabilities or code errors may still exist or the feature may not be enabled for that repository.

notes.front: What files can you download from security overview, and what are they for?
notes.back: Comma-separated values files of data from its pages, for security research and in-depth data analysis.
notes.explanation: The files can integrate easily with external datasets.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: From security overview, you can download comma-separated values (CSV) files containing data from several pages of your organization or enterprise's security overview. These files can be used for efforts like security research and in-depth data analysis, and can integrate easily with external datasets.

notes.front: Which security overview view visualises trends in the detection, remediation and prevention of security alerts?
notes.back: Overview.
notes.explanation: It is the dashboard view of the organisation’s security landscape and progress.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Overview:** visualize trends in **Detection**, **Remediation**, and **Prevention** of security alerts.

notes.front: Which security overview view lets you explore risk from vulnerable dependencies, code weaknesses or leaked secrets, across all alert types or one?
notes.back: Risk.
notes.explanation: It can cover every alert type or focus on a single one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Risk:** explore the risk from security alerts of all types or focus on a single alert type and identify your risk from specific vulnerable dependencies, code weaknesses, or leaked secrets

notes.front: Which security overview view assesses the adoption of security features across an organisation’s repositories?
notes.back: Coverage.
notes.explanation: It looks at which repositories use the features, rather than at alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Coverage:** assess the adoption of security features across repositories in the organization

notes.front: Which security overview view lets organisations on GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise run a free report that scans for leaked secrets?
notes.back: Assessments.
notes.explanation: The report is available whatever the enablement status of Advanced Security features.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Assessments:** regardless of the enablement status of Advanced Security features, organizations on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise can run a free report to scan the code in the organization for leaked secrets

notes.front: Which security overview view coordinates and measures targeted remediation efforts towards risk-reduction goals?
notes.back: Campaigns.
notes.explanation: It groups related security tasks across repositories and assigns owners.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Campaigns:** coordinate and measure targeted remediation efforts, grouping related security tasks across repositories, assigning owners, and tracking progress

notes.front: Which security overview view shows how quickly different teams are adopting security features?
notes.back: Enablement.
notes.explanation: It measures the pace of adoption by team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Enablement:** see how quickly different teams are adopting security features.

notes.front: Which security overview view assesses the impact of running CodeQL on pull requests?
notes.back: CodeQL pull requests.
notes.explanation: It also shows how development teams are resolving code scanning alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **CodeQL pull requests:** assess the impact of running CodeQL on pull requests and how development teams are resolving code scanning alerts

notes.front: Which security overview view helps you prioritise and track critical vulnerabilities, measuring security improvements across repositories?
notes.back: Dependabot.
notes.explanation: It follows vulnerabilities from identification through remediation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Dependabot**: prioritize and track critical vulnerabilities by identifying, remediating, and measuring security improvements across repositories.

notes.front: Which security overview view shows which types of secret push protection blocks, and which teams bypass it?
notes.back: Secret scanning.
notes.explanation: It links push protection blocks and bypasses to secret types and teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Secret scanning:** find out which types of secret are blocked by push protection and which teams are bypassing push protection

notes.front: Who can view security data across all repositories of an organisation in security overview?
notes.back: Organisation owners and security managers.
notes.explanation: What anyone else sees depends on their role and permissions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “Access to data in security overview”
notes.evidence: What you can see in security overview depends on your role and permissions in the organization or enterprise. In general: * Organization owners and security managers can view security data across all repositories in their organization.

notes.front: In security overview, which repositories can an ordinary organisation member see data for?
notes.back: Only repositories where they have access to security alerts.
notes.explanation: Security overview displays data only for repositories you have permission to view.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “Access to data in security overview”
notes.evidence: * Organization members can view data only for repositories where they have access to security alerts.

notes.front: What can enterprise owners see in the enterprise-level security overview?
notes.back: Aggregated data for organisations where they are an owner or security manager; repository detail needs the right organisation role.
notes.explanation: Enterprise ownership alone does not open repository-level detail.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “Access to data in security overview”
notes.evidence: * Enterprise owners can view aggregated security data in the enterprise-level security overview for organizations where they are an organization owner or security manager. To see repository-level details, they must have the appropriate role within the organization.

notes.front: Where do you find security overview for an enterprise, and what does it display?
notes.back: On the enterprise’s Security and quality tab; each page shows aggregated and repository-specific security information.
notes.explanation: Like the organisation version, it includes an overview dashboard of alert trends.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for enterprises”
notes.evidence: You can find security overview on the **shield Security and quality** tab for your enterprise. Each page displays aggregated and repository-specific security information for your enterprise.

notes.front: Which security campaign benefit makes sure developers hear about campaigns they can help with?
notes.back: Developers are notified about any campaigns they can contribute to.
notes.explanation: GitHub lists this among the benefits a campaign has over other ways of encouraging remediation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: Developers are notified about any security campaigns that they can contribute to. * Developers can see the alerts you've highlighted for remediation without leaving their normal workflows. * Each campaign has a named point of contact for questions, reviews, and collaboration.

notes.front: How do developers see the alerts that a security campaign highlights for them?
notes.back: Without leaving their normal workflows.
notes.explanation: The campaign also appears in the sidebar of each included repository’s Security and quality tab.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: Developers are notified about any security campaigns that they can contribute to. * Developers can see the alerts you've highlighted for remediation without leaving their normal workflows. * Each campaign has a named point of contact for questions, reviews, and collaboration.

notes.front: What does every security campaign have for questions, reviews and collaboration?
notes.back: A named point of contact.
notes.explanation: Those contacts are the campaign managers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: Developers are notified about any security campaigns that they can contribute to. * Developers can see the alerts you've highlighted for remediation without leaving their normal workflows. * Each campaign has a named point of contact for questions, reviews, and collaboration.

notes.front: What happens automatically for the code scanning alerts in a security campaign?
notes.back: Copilot Autofix is triggered to suggest a resolution.
notes.explanation: Secret scanning alerts in a campaign get no automatic remediation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: * For code scanning alerts, GitHub Copilot Autofix is automatically triggered to suggest a resolution. * For both code scanning and secret scanning, you can assign alerts in a campaign to users with write access or to Copilot cloud agent to automatically generate pull requests with fixes.

notes.front: To whom can you assign alerts in a security campaign so that pull requests with fixes are generated?
notes.back: Users with write access, or Copilot cloud agent.
notes.explanation: This works for both code scanning and secret scanning alerts in a campaign.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: * For code scanning alerts, GitHub Copilot Autofix is automatically triggered to suggest a resolution. * For both code scanning and secret scanning, you can assign alerts in a campaign to users with write access or to Copilot cloud agent to automatically generate pull requests with fixes.

notes.front: What does GitHub say is the advantage of using a template to pick closely related alerts for a campaign?
notes.back: Developers build on what they learn fixing one alert to fix several more.
notes.explanation: That gives developers an incentive to fix multiple alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Benefits of using security campaigns”
notes.evidence: You can use one of the templates to select a group of closely related alerts for a campaign. This allows developers to build on the knowledge gained by resolving one alert and use it to fix several more, providing them with an incentive to fix multiple alerts.

notes.front: When does GitHub notify a user about a code scanning or secret scanning alert assigned to them?
notes.back: When they are assigned to it, and when that alert is dismissed.
notes.explanation: Only users with write access to the repository can be assigned in the first place.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “About assigning alerts to users and Copilot cloud agent”
notes.evidence: GitHub notifies users: * When they are assigned to an alert * When that alert is dismissed

notes.front: Security campaigns for secret scanning alerts are in {{c1::public preview}} and subject to change.
notes.explanation: The creation workflow is the same for code and secret campaigns; progress tracking and the developer experience differ.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Differences between code and secret campaigns”
notes.evidence: Campaigns for secret scanning alerts are currently in public preview and are subject to change. The creation workflow is the same for all campaigns, but you will notice a few differences in progress tracking and developer experience.

notes.front: Which type of security campaign supports repository tracking issues?
notes.back: Code campaigns; secret campaigns do not.
notes.explanation: On the Publish campaign page, a code campaign can create a campaign issue in each included repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Differences between code and secret campaigns”
notes.evidence: | Repository tracking issues | Supported | Not supported |

notes.front: Which type of security campaign has automatic remediation support, and through what?
notes.back: Code campaigns, through Copilot Autofix; secret campaigns have none.
notes.explanation: Every alert in a new code campaign is submitted to Copilot Autofix.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Differences between code and secret campaigns”
notes.evidence: | Automatic remediation support | Supported GitHub Copilot Autofix | Not supported |

notes.front: What happens when a secret scanning alert is assigned to someone who cannot view the alert list?
notes.back: Their permissions are temporarily raised for that alert, and revoked when they are unassigned.
notes.explanation: This is why the docs say assignment in secret campaigns “may raise permissions”.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “About assigning alerts to users and Copilot cloud agent”
notes.evidence: If the assignee for a secret scanning alert **cannot view the alert list**, their permissions are temporarily raised for that alert. Any additional permissions are revoked when they are unassigned from the alert.

notes.front: From where are security campaigns created and managed?
notes.back: The organisation’s Security and quality tab, under Campaigns.
notes.explanation: Campaigns are managed from the security overview for the organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Creating a security campaign”
notes.evidence: Security campaigns are created and managed from the **shield Security and quality** tab for your organization.

notes.front: What are the two ways of choosing the alerts for a new security campaign?
notes.back: Campaign templates, which hold filters for the most common selections, or custom filters that you define.
notes.explanation: When agentic autofix is disabled, templates also use `autofix:supported` to keep only alerts that Copilot Autofix supports.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Creating a security campaign”
notes.evidence: Campaign templates contain filters for the most common alert selections. When agentic autofix is disabled, they also use `autofix:supported` to include only alerts for rules supported by GitHub Copilot Autofix. * **Custom filters**: Creating a campaign using custom filters lets you define your own criteria

notes.front: How many alerts can one security campaign include?
notes.back: 1,000 alerts or fewer.
notes.explanation: You review the set of alerts and adjust the filters until the campaign is within that limit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: Review the set of alerts to be included in the campaign, and adjust the filters as necessary. Make sure you have chosen 1000 alerts or fewer.

notes.front: When saving a new campaign’s scope, when should you choose Draft campaign rather than Publish campaign?
notes.back: When you plan to review its scope and details before launch, or want feedback on it.
notes.explanation: Publish campaign is for when you don’t need a review phase.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: If you plan to review the scope and details of the campaign prior to launch, or seek feedback on the implementation of the campaign, click **issue-draft Draft campaign**. * If you intend to publish the campaign, and don't need a review phase, click **goal Publish campaign**.

notes.front: What happens to the alerts when you create a code campaign?
notes.back: They are all submitted automatically to Copilot Autofix, to be processed as capacity allows.
notes.explanation: Processing as capacity allows keeps suggestions for alerts in pull requests from being delayed by a new campaign.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Launching a security campaign”
notes.evidence: When you create a code campaign, all the alerts are automatically submitted to GitHub Copilot Autofix to be processed as capacity allows. This ensures that suggestions for alerts found in pull requests aren't delayed by a new campaign.

notes.front: How many security campaigns can be active at once in an organisation?
notes.back: Ten.
notes.explanation: You should close a campaign when it is complete or when you want to pause it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Closing, reopening and deleting security campaigns”
notes.evidence: There is a limit of 10 active campaigns. When a campaign is complete, or if you want to pause it, you should close it.

notes.front: What are two tools GitHub provides for auditing responses to security alerts?
notes.back: Any two of: historical timelines, security overview, audit logs, the API, webhooks.
notes.explanation: Auditors use them to check that alerts are being resolved properly and to find areas for more training.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “About security tools for auditors”
notes.evidence: This guide describes the tools, which include historical timelines, security overview, audit logs, the API, and webhooks. Security auditors can use these tools to ensure the appropriate actions are being taken to resolve security alerts and to identify areas for additional training.

notes.front: Does a security alert timeline record status changes made by automation?
notes.back: Yes: every status change is recorded, whatever caused it, such as Dependabot closing a fixed alert.
notes.explanation: Changes made by people, such as a developer reopening an alert, are recorded too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Security alert timelines”
notes.evidence: When the status of an alert changes this is recorded on the timeline, regardless of what caused the change, for example, Dependabot closing a fixed alert and a developer reopening an alert.

notes.front: Which secret scanning activities create audit log events?
notes.back: An alert being created, resolved or reopened, and push protection being bypassed.
notes.explanation: Many timeline events also create an event in the audit log.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Audit log”
notes.evidence: * Secret scanning events track when an alert is created, resolved, or reopened, also when push protection is bypassed. * Dependabot events track when an alert is created, dismissed, or resolved. * Code scanning does not create timeline events in an audit log.

notes.front: Which Dependabot alert activities create audit log events?
notes.back: An alert being created, dismissed or resolved.
notes.explanation: Events can be triggered manually or by automation, such as Dependabot creating an alert.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Audit log”
notes.evidence: * Secret scanning events track when an alert is created, resolved, or reopened, also when push protection is bypassed. * Dependabot events track when an alert is created, dismissed, or resolved. * Code scanning does not create timeline events in an audit log.

notes.front: Does code scanning create timeline events in the audit log?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: A code scanning alert’s history is on its security alert timeline instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Audit log”
notes.evidence: * Secret scanning events track when an alert is created, resolved, or reopened, also when push protection is bypassed. * Dependabot events track when an alert is created, dismissed, or resolved. * Code scanning does not create timeline events in an audit log.

notes.front: Which three webhooks can you set up to receive payloads whenever there is a response to a security alert?
notes.back: `code_scanning_alert`, `dependabot_alert` and `secret_scanning_alert`.
notes.explanation: They work in an organisation or a repository, and you can choose which responses to act on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Webhooks”
notes.evidence: You can set up `code_scanning_alert`, `dependabot_alert`, and `secret_scanning_alert` webhooks to receive payloads whenever there is a response to a security alert in an organization or repository.

notes.front: Which alert property lets a webhook track secret scanning alerts created when someone bypasses push protection?
notes.back: `"push_protection_bypassed": true`.
notes.explanation: The same property filters the secret scanning alerts API for push protection bypasses.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Webhooks”
notes.evidence: you might want to define a webhook that tracks secret scanning alerts created when someone bypasses push protection using the alert property `"push_protection_bypassed": true`.

notes.front: What status information about a security alert does the API report?
notes.back: Only the alert’s current status.
notes.explanation: For the history of changes, the alert’s timeline is the record.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “API”
notes.evidence: You can also use the API to make additional updates to the alert or to automate follow-up actions, such as creating a new issue for each alert that needs further action. Only the current status of an alert is reported by the API.

notes.front: At which levels can you list code scanning alerts through the API?
notes.back: For a repository, an organisation or an enterprise.
notes.explanation: Path parameters narrow the list to alerts meeting specific criteria; the Dependabot and secret scanning alert APIs work the same way.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Code scanning alerts API”
notes.evidence: You can list all code scanning alerts for a repository, organization, or enterprise, or use path parameters to list only alerts that meet a specific set of criteria.

notes.front: Which webhook event does GitHub send when a Dependabot alert’s assignees change?
notes.back: `assignees_changed`.
notes.explanation: You can use it to trigger workflows or to sync assignment data with external systems.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependabot alerts”, “Alert ownership and assignments”
notes.evidence: When an alert's assignees change, GitHub sends an `assignees_changed` webhook event. You can use this event to trigger workflows or sync assignment data with external systems.

notes.front: Where can you read or set a Dependabot alert’s dismissal comment programmatically?
notes.back: Through the GraphQL API, in the `dismissComment` field.
notes.explanation: The same comment appears on the alert timeline as justification for auditing.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing and updating Dependabot alerts”, “Dismissing Dependabot alerts”
notes.evidence: Optionally, add a dismissal comment. The dismissal comment will be added to the alert timeline and can be used as justification during auditing and reporting. You can retrieve or set a comment by using the GraphQL API. The comment is contained in the `dismissComment` field.

notes.front: Where can you read or set a code scanning alert’s dismissal comment programmatically?
notes.back: Through the code scanning API, in `dismissed_comment` for the `alerts/{alert_number}` endpoint.
notes.explanation: As with other alerts, the comment is added to the alert timeline for auditing and reporting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: The dismissal comment is added to the alert timeline and can be used as justification during auditing and reporting. You can retrieve or set a comment by using the code scanning REST API. The comment is contained in `dismissed_comment` for the `alerts/{alert_number}` endpoint.

notes.front: When closing a secret scanning alert, where do you add a dismissal comment?
notes.back: In the optional “Comment” field, after choosing a reason under “Close as”.
notes.explanation: The comment is added to the alert timeline for auditing and reporting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving alerts from secret scanning”, “Closing alerts”
notes.evidence: Optionally, in the "Comment" field, add a dismissal comment. The dismissal comment will be added to the alert timeline and can be used as justification during auditing and reporting.

notes.front: Security overview shows no code scanning alerts for a repository. A manager concludes the repository has no vulnerabilities. What should you tell them?
notes.back: A) Not necessarily: problems may be undetected, or code scanning may not be enabled there
notes.choices:
A) Not necessarily: problems may be undetected, or code scanning may not be enabled there
B) Correct, but only for public repositories
C) Correct: no alerts means clean code
D) The data has not loaded yet
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: GitHub warns that undetected vulnerabilities may still exist. D: nothing suggests a loading problem; an empty list is a normal state.
notes.explanation: Security overview shows only active alerts raised by features that are running.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: If there are no alerts shown in security overview for a repository, undetected security vulnerabilities or code errors may still exist or the feature may not be enabled for that repository.

notes.front: A vulnerable dependency exists only on a long-running `feature` branch, not on the default branch. Will security overview’s figures include its alert?
notes.back: B) No: security overview shows default branches only
notes.choices:
A) Yes: all branches are aggregated
B) No: security overview shows default branches only
C) Only in the Risk view
D) Only once a campaign includes it
notes.choicesExplained: A: the views cover default branches only. C: the Risk view is limited to default branches like every other view. D: campaigns do not change what the views show.
notes.explanation: All security overview views show information and metrics for default branches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: All views show information and metrics for the **default** branches of the repositories you have permission to view in an organization or enterprise.

notes.front: An organisation member has access to security alerts in 2 of its 40 repositories. What do they see in security overview?
notes.back: B) Data for the 2 repositories
notes.choices:
A) Data for all 40 repositories
B) Data for the 2 repositories
C) Data for public repositories only
D) Nothing: only owners can open security overview
notes.choicesExplained: A: organisation-wide data is for owners and security managers. D: members can use it for repositories where they have alert access. C: visibility follows alert access, not repository visibility.
notes.explanation: Security overview shows data only for repositories you have permission to view.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “Access to data in security overview”
notes.evidence: * Organization members can view data only for repositories where they have access to security alerts.

notes.front: A security director wants to compare how quickly different teams are taking up security features. Which security overview view fits?
notes.back: A) Enablement
notes.choices:
A) Enablement
B) Risk
C) CodeQL pull requests
D) Secret scanning
notes.choicesExplained: B: Risk explores risk from alerts. C: shows the impact of CodeQL on pull requests. D: covers push protection blocks and bypasses.
notes.explanation: Enablement shows the pace of adoption by team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Enablement:** see how quickly different teams are adopting security features.

notes.front: An analyst wants to combine security overview data with an external dataset in their own analysis tool. What should they use?
notes.back: A) Comma-separated values files downloaded from security overview
notes.choices:
A) Comma-separated values files downloaded from security overview
B) Each alert’s security alert timeline
C) Screenshots of the Overview dashboard
D) The Assessments view
notes.choicesExplained: C: screenshots are not data. B: timelines record one alert at a time. D: Assessments runs a report on leaked secrets, not an export.
notes.explanation: The downloads are meant for in-depth analysis and integrate easily with external datasets.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About the views”
notes.evidence: These files can be used for efforts like security research and in-depth data analysis, and can integrate easily with external datasets.

notes.front: A security lead’s campaign filters match 1,400 alerts. What must they do before saving the campaign?
notes.back: B) Narrow the filters to 1,000 alerts or fewer
notes.choices:
A) Save it: GitHub keeps the first 1,000
B) Narrow the filters to 1,000 alerts or fewer
C) Split the alerts between the campaign managers
D) Ask an enterprise owner to raise the limit
notes.choicesExplained: A: the docs describe no automatic trimming. C: managers are contacts, not containers for alerts. D: the docs describe no way to raise the limit.
notes.explanation: You adjust the filters as necessary until the campaign holds 1,000 alerts or fewer.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: Review the set of alerts to be included in the campaign, and adjust the filters as necessary. Make sure you have chosen 1000 alerts or fewer.

notes.front: An organisation already has 10 active campaigns, one of them finished, and wants to start another. What should it do?
notes.back: A) Close the finished campaign, then create the new one
notes.choices:
A) Close the finished campaign, then create the new one
B) Create a second organisation
C) Add the new alerts to the finished campaign
D) Merge two active campaigns into one
notes.choicesExplained: B: unnecessary; closing a campaign frees a place. C: a finished campaign should be closed, not reused. D: the docs describe no merging of campaigns.
notes.explanation: There is a limit of 10 active campaigns, and a complete campaign should be closed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Closing, reopening and deleting security campaigns”
notes.evidence: There is a limit of 10 active campaigns. When a campaign is complete, or if you want to pause it, you should close it.

notes.front: A security lead wants to name a developer who has write access to the included repositories as a campaign manager. Is that allowed?
notes.back: B) No: campaign managers must be organisation owners or security managers
notes.choices:
A) Yes: any member with write access qualifies
B) No: campaign managers must be organisation owners or security managers
C) Only if the developer created the campaign
D) Yes, once the developer is added as a collaborator
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: repository access is not the test. C: creating the campaign does not qualify anyone.
notes.explanation: Write access lets someone be assigned campaign alerts, but not manage the campaign.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: Campaign managers must be users or teams that are owners or security managers in the organization.

notes.front: A lead running a secret scanning campaign wants a tracking issue in each repository and Copilot Autofix suggestions. What will they get?
notes.back: D) Neither: secret campaigns support no tracking issues and no automatic remediation
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) Tracking issues only
C) Autofix suggestions only
D) Neither: secret campaigns support no tracking issues and no automatic remediation
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: both features are listed as supported for code campaigns only.
notes.explanation: Tracking issues and Copilot Autofix belong to code campaigns.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “Differences between code and secret campaigns”
notes.evidence: | Repository tracking issues | Supported | Not supported |

notes.front: A security lead wants the application security team to comment on a campaign’s scope before any developer is notified. What should they do?
notes.back: B) Save it as a draft campaign
notes.choices:
A) Publish it, then close it straight away
B) Save it as a draft campaign
C) Publish it without campaign managers
D) Download its alerts as a file
notes.choicesExplained: A: publishing notifies developers. C: publishing still notifies developers, and managers are part of the details. D: an export doesn’t give the team a campaign to review.
notes.explanation: A draft is for reviewing scope and details, or seeking feedback, before launch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Create a campaign”
notes.evidence: If you plan to review the scope and details of the campaign prior to launch, or seek feedback on the implementation of the campaign, click **issue-draft Draft campaign**.

notes.front: An auditor needs to see when a code scanning alert was reopened after being dismissed. Where should they look?
notes.back: B) The alert’s security alert timeline
notes.choices:
A) The organisation’s audit log
B) The alert’s security alert timeline
C) The alert through the code scanning API
D) Security overview’s Overview dashboard
notes.choicesExplained: A: code scanning does not create timeline events in the audit log. C: the API reports only the current status. D: the dashboard shows aggregated trends, not one alert’s history.
notes.explanation: The timeline records every status change of the alert, whatever caused it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Audit log”
notes.evidence: * Secret scanning events track when an alert is created, resolved, or reopened, also when push protection is bypassed. * Dependabot events track when an alert is created, dismissed, or resolved. * Code scanning does not create timeline events in an audit log.

notes.front: A team wants a chat message whenever a secret scanning alert is created because someone bypassed push protection. What should they set up?
notes.back: D) A `secret_scanning_alert` webhook acting on `"push_protection_bypassed": true`
notes.choices:
A) A `code_scanning_alert` webhook
B) A `dependabot_alert` webhook
C) A weekly search of the security alert timelines
D) A `secret_scanning_alert` webhook acting on `"push_protection_bypassed": true`
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: those webhooks cover other alert types. C: a weekly search is not a notification whenever a bypass happens.
notes.explanation: Webhook payloads can be passed to the tools a team uses, and the property singles out bypasses.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “Webhooks”
notes.evidence: You can also define which responses to act on, for example, you might want to define a webhook that tracks secret scanning alerts created when someone bypasses push protection using the alert property `"push_protection_bypassed": true`.

notes.front: A script calls the API to rebuild the full history of an alert’s dismissals and reopenings. What will it get?
notes.back: D) Only the alert’s current status; the history is on its timeline
notes.choices:
A) The full history of every status change
B) Every dismissal comment ever written
C) The history, but only for code scanning alerts
D) Only the alert’s current status; the history is on its timeline
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the API reports only the current status, for every alert type. B: a comment is part of the alert’s current state, not a history of changes.
notes.explanation: The security alert timeline records each change of status.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Auditing security alerts”, “API”
notes.evidence: Only the current status of an alert is reported by the API.

notes.front: A developer dismisses a Dependabot alert as a tolerable risk. Months later an auditor asks why. What should the developer have done?
notes.back: D) Added a dismissal comment, which is kept on the alert timeline
notes.choices:
A) Emailed the security team
B) Explained it in a commit message
C) Nothing: the chosen reason is stored with a full explanation
D) Added a dismissal comment, which is kept on the alert timeline
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: neither is attached to the alert. C: the reason is a single choice; the comment is what records context.
notes.explanation: The dismissal comment can be used as justification during auditing and reporting.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing and updating Dependabot alerts”, “Dismissing Dependabot alerts”
notes.evidence: Optionally, add a dismissal comment. The dismissal comment will be added to the alert timeline and can be used as justification during auditing and reporting. You can retrieve or set a comment by using the GraphQL API. The comment is contained in the `dismissComment` field.

notes.front: A security lead wants to assign a code scanning alert in a campaign to a developer who has only read access to the repository. What do the docs say?
notes.back: C) Not possible: code scanning alerts can be assigned only to users with write access
notes.choices:
A) Assign it: their permissions are raised temporarily
B) Assign it to their team instead
C) Not possible: code scanning alerts can be assigned only to users with write access
D) Code scanning alerts cannot be assigned at all
notes.choicesExplained: A: temporary raising applies to secret scanning alerts. B: the docs describe assigning users with write access, not teams. D: code scanning alerts can be assigned.
notes.explanation: Only a secret scanning alert raises an assignee’s permissions, and only if they cannot view the alert list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About security campaigns”, “About assigning alerts to users and Copilot cloud agent”
notes.evidence: You can assign a code scanning or secret scanning alert to any user who has **write** access for the repository. If the assignee for a secret scanning alert **cannot view the alert list**, their permissions are temporarily raised for that alert.

notes.front: How does security overview’s Coverage view differ from its Enablement view?
notes.back: Coverage assesses which repositories have adopted security features; Enablement shows how quickly different teams are adopting them.
notes.explanation: One is a snapshot of adoption across repositories, the other a measure of its pace by team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Security overview”, “About security overview for organizations”
notes.evidence: * **Coverage:** assess the adoption of security features across repositories in the organization, see [Assessing adoption of security features](/en/code-security/how-tos/view-and-interpret-data/analyze-organization-data/assessing-adoption-code-security).

notes.front: Who is notified when a code campaign starts, compared with a secret campaign?
notes.back: Code: anyone with write access to an included repository. Secret: anyone who can see the repository’s alert list.
notes.explanation: In both cases the campaign also appears in the repository’s Security and quality tab sidebar.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “How developers know a security campaign has started”
notes.evidence: * **Code campaigns**: Anyone with **write** access to a repository included in the campaign is notified. * **Secret campaigns**: Anyone with access to see the alert list view for a repository included in the campaign is notified.

notes.front: What is the difference between closing and deleting a security campaign?
notes.back: A closed campaign stays in the Closed list and can be reopened; deleting it removes the campaign and its data.
notes.explanation: Delete only when you don’t need to keep the campaign or its data.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating and managing security campaigns”, “Closing, reopening and deleting security campaigns”
notes.evidence: You can still view all closed campaigns in the "Closed" campaign list, and you can reopen a closed campaign. If you don't need to retain the campaign or its data, you can delete it.

notes.front: Which field holds the dismissal comment of a Dependabot alert, and which that of a code scanning alert?
notes.back: `dismissComment` in the GraphQL API for Dependabot; `dismissed_comment` in the code scanning API.
notes.explanation: Both comments end up on the alert timeline as justification for auditing.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Viewing and updating Dependabot alerts”, “Dismissing Dependabot alerts”
notes.evidence: You can retrieve or set a comment by using the GraphQL API. The comment is contained in the `dismissComment` field.
